title: Do, not Be is the operative word
author: Erica Kleinknecht
summary: Developmental psychologist Erica Kleinknecht reacts to a Peter Gray post blaming school, rather than phones, for children's distress, and argues that critique needs actionable fixes. Her proposal is small but, she says, profound: career readiness starts too soon, and schools that ask children who they want to be push them toward identity labels before they have had experiences to build an identity on. She draws on Marjorie Rhodes' work, in which a New York field experiment compared teachers who framed a science lesson as being scientists with those who framed it as doing science. Children invited to do science showed greater interest and efficacy over the year, while being language tended to prompt the question of whether the child fits the group. Her practical advice is to change the language and not the curriculum: ask what children want to do, say let's write some poems rather than let's be poets, and replace career readiness with exploration such as scavenger hunts about what people do in different jobs. She closes by arguing that adults should shape experiences rather than identities and let children be their age.
points: Asking children who they want to be invites a yes or no on identity, and a label adopted early produces a foreclosed identity that is brittle, whereas one that emerges from varied experience is committed and secure.
In the Rhodes field experiment, a lesson framed as doing science raised later interest and efficacy compared with the same lesson framed as being scientists.
Identity language draws attention to group membership, so children who do not see a resemblance may feel they do not belong and disengage.
The fix is cheap and immediate: reword prompts from be to do and swap career-readiness exercises for exploratory activities, with no curriculum change required.
Critique of schooling lands better when paired with actionable steps, which is why the author offers a language-level change rather than only calling for more play.
quotes: Career readiness is starting too soon. Schools (middle school, in my local district, and then again in high school) are forcing kids to think too much, too soon, about being, at the expense of doing.

When we ask children “identity” questions we are inviting a “yes” or a “no” – “no, I’m not like that”, for example. A more effective approach is to offer up opportunities to do, and then let children naturally decide how that doing feels.

Identity takes years to develop and healthy identities are those that emerge from experiences. When young people adopt a label and then act in kind, their identity is foreclosed: brittle, uneasy, and insecure.

Children who were invited to do science in that one-off activity over the course of the year showed greater interest in and greater efficacy of accomplishment, in science-related schoolwork and activities. The effect was powerful!

When we signal identity, we are drawing attention to group-level dimensions, and kids are thinking: “do I fit with that group?” If children don’t see a resemblance, then they feel like they don’t belong, and anxiety or disinterest is activated.
Instead of who do you want to be when you grow up, we should simply say what do you want to do when you grow up? Instead of “let’s be poets” for the writing workshop, we say “let’s write some poems
This kind of change can happen right away! No need to change the curriculum — just change the language and the adjust the activities that already exist.
